facts.fact: The Theme Building was designed by Luckman with his former partner Pereira and Welton Becket of Los Angeles.
facts.quote: Luckman, along with his former partner, Pereira, and Welton Becket of Los Angeles, were contracted to design the Theme Building.

facts.fact: Pereira and Luckman designed the Theme Building at Los Angeles International Airport in collaboration with Paul Williams and Welton Becket.
facts.quote: The duo designed some of Los Angeles's most well-known buildings, including the famed "Theme Building" at Los Angeles International Airport (in collaboration with Paul Williams and Welton Becket).

facts.fact: It was part of a $50 million revamp of Los Angeles International Airport that began in April 1960.
facts.quote: In April 1960, a $50 million overall revamp project of the airport, known as the "Los Angeles Jet Age Terminal Construction Project", began at the Los Angeles International Airport.

facts.fact: Luckman had the concept in mind since 1953.
facts.quote: The Theme Building was a concept that Luckman had in mind since 1953.

facts.fact: In the original idea it was a much larger glass dome meant to hold the airport's main ticketing area and terminals.
facts.quote: In the original conception, the Theme Building was to be a much larger structure that would have consisted primarily of a glass dome that was meant to be LAX's main ticketing area and terminals.

facts.fact: It was to have a revolving restaurant with a 360-degree view, but the mechanism proved too costly to maintain and the restaurant became stationary.
facts.quote: The Theme Building would have also hosted a revolving restaurant, giving patrons a 360-degree view of the surrounding area. The mechanism soon proved to be too costly to maintain, and the restaurant became stationary.

facts.fact: The Theme Building opened to the public in 1961.
facts.quote: The Theme Building opened to the public in 1961.

facts.fact: It is a former Enco service station at the foot of Tramway Road, the road to the Palm Springs Aerial Tramway.
facts.quote: The Tramway Gas Station is a landmark former Enco service station in Palm Springs, California, United States, so named because of its location at the foot of Tramway Road, the lone road leading to the base of the Palm Springs Aerial Tramway.

facts.fact: It was meant to be the first Palm Springs building visitors saw when arriving from the north.
facts.quote: It was intended to be the first Palm Springs building visitors saw when approaching the city from the north via California State Route 111.

facts.fact: Albert Frey and Robson C. Chambers designed it in 1965, with a cantilevered, wedge-shaped canopy described as a hyperbolic paraboloid.
facts.quote: The building, with its distinctive, cantilevered, wedge-shaped canopy (referred to as a hyperbolic paraboloid on a historic marker mounted on the building) was built in 1965 and designed by Albert Frey and Robson C. Chambers.

facts.fact: It is considered a prime example of modernist architecture.
facts.quote: It is considered to be a prime example of modernist architecture.

facts.fact: Since 2003 it has been the Palm Springs Visitor Center, and it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.
facts.quote: Since 2003 it has been operated by the Palm Springs Bureau of Tourism as the Palm Springs Visitor Center. The building was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.

facts.fact: The station is credited to the firm of Clark, Frey and Chambers, at the bottom of the tramway entrance road.
facts.quote: The firm of Clark, Frey and Chambers also designed the iconic Tramway Gas Station at the bottom of the entrance road.

facts.fact: Wayfarers Chapel, called "The Glass Church", was designed by Lloyd Wright for a site in Rancho Palos Verdes, California.
facts.quote: Wayfarers Chapel, or "The Glass Church", is a disassembled chapel designed by Lloyd Wright and originally located in Rancho Palos Verdes, California.

facts.fact: Its organic architecture sat on a bluff above the Pacific Ocean, and it was a Swedenborgian memorial to Emanuel Swedenborg.
facts.quote: The chapel had unique organic architecture sited on a bluff above the Pacific Ocean. Affiliated with the Swedenborgian Church of North America, it served as a memorial to the 18th-century scientist and theosopher Emanuel Swedenborg.

facts.fact: The 100-seat church was designed in the late 1940s by Lloyd Wright, son of Frank Lloyd Wright, and built between 1949 and 1951 for $25,000.
facts.quote: The 100-seat church was designed by Lloyd Wright (son of Frank Lloyd Wright) in the late 1940s and was built between 1949 and 1951, at a cost of $25,000.

facts.fact: It is an indoor/outdoor structure made almost entirely of glass.
facts.quote: His best-known project is the Wayfarers Chapel, also known as "The Glass Church", an indoor/outdoor structure made almost entirely of glass and built in 1951 for the Swedenborgian church, overlooking the Pacific Ocean on the Palos Verdes Peninsula.

facts.fact: Wright avoided masonry to make a delicate enclosure in which the landscape defines the sacred space.
facts.quote: Wright departed from the tradition of using masonry in order to "achieve a delicate enclosure that allows the surrounding landscape to define the sacred space".

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2005 and became a National Historic Landmark in 2023.
facts.quote: The Wayfarers Chapel was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 2005 and was designated a National Historic Landmark for its architecture and landscaping in 2023.

facts.fact: Land movement damaged it, and it was dismantled in 2024 and stored.
facts.quote: Built in 1949, the chapel was dismantled in 2024 and carefully stored after extreme earth movement had damaged the structure.

facts.fact: In 2025 the chapel was working to rebuild at the Battery Barnes site, about a mile west of the original location.
facts.quote: The prospective location is at the Battery Barnes military site near Rancho Palos Verdes City Hall, about 1 mile (1.6 km) west of the original location.

facts.fact: The Koerner House in Palm Springs was designed in 1955 for Leon and Thea Koerner of Vancouver.
facts.quote: The house was designed in 1955 for the Vancouver-based couple of Leon Koerner and Thea Koerner.

facts.fact: It is a fine example of the houses E. Stewart Williams designed from 1947 to the end of the 1960s.
facts.quote: The house is a fine example of the residences that master architect E. Stewart Williams designed between 1947 and the end of the 1960s.

facts.fact: The single-storey house has a shed roof, deep overhangs and large glass areas with sliding doors for indoor-outdoor flow.
facts.quote: The single-story structure features a shed roof, deep overhangs, and large glass surface areas with sliding glass doors that facilitate its indoor-outdoor flow.

facts.fact: The landscaping was designed by Eckbo, Royston and Williams.
facts.quote: The landscaping was designed by Eckbo, Royston and Williams.

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2016.
facts.quote: The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2016.

facts.fact: Reunion Tower is a 561 ft (171 m) observation tower in Dallas and one of its best-known landmarks.
facts.quote: Reunion Tower is a 561 ft (171 m) observation tower in Dallas, and one of the city's most recognizable landmarks.

facts.fact: It was designed by Welton Becket & Associates.
facts.quote: It was designed by architectural firm Welton Becket & Associates.

facts.fact: Known locally as "The Ball", it was completed on 2 February 1978 with the Hyatt Regency Dallas as part of an urban redevelopment that also renovated Union Station.
facts.quote: Reunion Tower, also known locally as "The Ball",  was completed on February 2, 1978, along with the Hyatt Regency Dallas at Reunion, as part of an urban redevelopment project that also renovated the historic Union Station, which today services Amtrak, Dallas Area Rapid Transit, and the Trinity Railway Express to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport and Fort Worth.

facts.fact: Three circular floors sit on four shafts of poured-in-place concrete.
facts.quote: The tower contains three floors with circular floor plans on top of four shafts of poured-in-place concrete.

facts.fact: A central shaft holds stairs and equipment, and three rectangular shafts with glass outer walls carry the elevators.
facts.quote: A central cylindrical shaft houses both stairs and mechanical equipment. Three rectangular shafts, featuring elevators, rise parallel to the central shaft.

facts.fact: The top three floors sit inside an open-air geodesic sphere of aluminium struts.
facts.quote: The top three floors are encased in an open-air sphere, which is a geodesic dome formed with aluminum struts.

facts.fact: In 2011 its incandescent lights were replaced by 259 programmable LED fixtures for light shows.
facts.quote: In 2011, these were replaced with a programmable LED lighting system consisting of 259 RGB LED fixtures, allowing the tower to display animated light shows, holiday displays, sports celebrations, and civic messages.

facts.fact: Landscape architect Angela Danadjieva is known for her work with Lawrence Halprin & Associates, including Freeway Park in Seattle.
facts.quote: She is well known for her work with Lawrence Halprin & Associates, including the Ira Keller Fountain in Portland, Oregon and Freeway Park in Seattle, Washington.

facts.fact: Danadjieva was the lead designer of Freeway Park.
facts.quote: Notably, she was lead designer on the Ira Keller Fountain Park in Portland, Oregon, and Freeway Park in Seattle, Washington.

facts.fact: Her later firm, Danadjieva & Koenig Associates, extended Freeway Park to include the Washington State Convention and Trade Center.
facts.quote: Their major projects include the White River State Park in Indianapolis, Indiana, a planning study for James River Park System in Richmond, Virginia, and an extension to Seattle's Freeway Park to include the Washington State Convention and Trade Center.

facts.fact: The Tacoma Dome is an indoor multi-purpose arena in Tacoma, Washington, south of downtown next to Interstate 5.
facts.quote: The Tacoma Dome is an indoor multi-purpose arena in Tacoma, Washington, United States. It is located south of Downtown Tacoma, adjacent to Interstate 5 and Tacoma Dome Station.

facts.fact: It was designed by local architects Jim McGranahan and Lyn Messenger, who won an international design competition, and cost $44 million.
facts.quote: It was designed by local architects Jim McGranahan and Lyn Messenger, who won an international design competition, and cost $44 million to construct.

facts.fact: It opened on 21 April 1983.
facts.quote: It opened on April 21, 1983, with 25,000 people attending the opening ceremonies.

facts.fact: The arena is 530 ft (160 m) across and 152 ft (46 m) high, and seats 20,722 for basketball.
facts.quote: At 530 feet (160 m) in diameter and 152 feet (46 m) in height, the arena seats 20,722 for basketball games, with a maximum capacity of 21,000.

facts.fact: When it opened it was the world's largest arena with a wooden dome by volume.
facts.quote: It was the largest arena with a wooden dome in the world by volume at the time of its opening; the Superior Dome in Marquette, Michigan, opened in 1991 with a larger-diameter geodesic dome at 536 feet (163 m), but is 143 feet (44 m) high and seats a maximum of 16,000.

facts.fact: The roof weighs 1.44 million pounds, and some of its planks came from timber felled after the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens.
facts.quote: The dome's roof weighs 1.44 million pounds (650 t); some of the planks that form the roof were sourced from felled timber following the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens.

facts.fact: It has little fixed seating so that seating and the playing field can be arranged flexibly.
facts.quote: Unlike most other arenas of its size, the arena contains little in the way of fixed seating, so as to maximize the flexibility of the seating arrangements and the shape of the playing field.

facts.fact: The Tempe Municipal Building is Tempe's city hall, shaped as an inverted pyramid.
facts.quote: The Tempe Municipal Building is an inverted pyramid-shaped building which serves as the city hall of Tempe, Arizona.

facts.fact: It was designed by Rolf Osland, Michael Goodwin and Kemper Goodwin and built in 1969–1971.
facts.quote: It was designed by architects Rolf Osland, Michael Goodwin and Kemper Goodwin, and built during 1969–1971.

facts.fact: Goodwin's first design, a large concrete building like Boston City Hall, was rejected by the city council.
facts.quote: The first design Michael Goodwin proposed was a large concrete building, similar to Boston City Hall. The city council rejected his design.

facts.fact: The inverted pyramid shape helps keep the building cool in summer and warm in winter.
facts.quote: The building's inverted pyramidal shape helps in keeping the building cool in summer and warm in winter.

facts.fact: Floors grow upward: 2,025 sq ft on the ground floor, 5,625 on the second and 10,000 on the third.
facts.quote: The ground floor comprises only 2,025 square feet (188.1 m2) of reception space, while the second floor is 5,625 square feet (522.6 m2) and the third floor 10,000 square feet (930 m2).

facts.fact: The council chambers are in a semi-buried basement, and free-standing fire stair towers flank the building.
facts.quote: The council chambers are in a semi-buried basement level. The building is flanked by free-standing fire stair towers.

facts.fact: It was completed and inaugurated on 2 October 1971.
facts.quote: The building was completed in 1971 and inaugurated on October 2 of that year.

facts.fact: The Solar Building in Albuquerque was the world's first commercial building heated mainly by solar energy.
facts.quote: The Solar Building, located in Albuquerque, New Mexico, was the world's first commercial building to be heated primarily by solar energy.

facts.fact: It was built in 1956 for the engineers Bridgers & Paxton, who designed its heating system.
facts.quote: It was built in 1956 to house the engineering firm of Bridgers & Paxton, who were responsible for the heating system design.

facts.fact: Stanley & Wright were the architects; the building cost $58,500, about $15,000 of it for heating and cooling.
facts.quote: Stanley & Wright were the architects for the building. Its total cost was $58,500, of which the heating and cooling system made up about $15,000—roughly twice the cost of a conventional system.

facts.fact: It is a one-storey International Style building in two main sections.
facts.quote: The Solar Building is a one-story, International Style building consisting of two main sections.

facts.fact: The north wing's roof and south wall are angled at 20 and 30 degrees to give the solar collectors high southern exposure.
facts.quote: It has an irregular quadrilateral cross-section with the roof and south wall both angled (at 20 and 30 degrees, respectively) in order to provide a high southern exposure for the solar collectors.

facts.fact: An array of 56 solar collectors totalling 800 sq ft sat on the south wall.
facts.quote: The building's active solar heating system employed an array of 56 solar thermal collectors with a total area of 800 square feet (74 m2).

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1989, only 33 years after it was built.
facts.quote: It was added to the New Mexico State Register of Cultural Properties in 1985 and the National Register of Historic Places in 1989, only 33 years after it was built.

facts.fact: The Fort Worth Water Gardens is a 4.3-acre urban park at the south end of downtown Fort Worth, beside the convention center.
facts.quote: It covers 4.3-acres (1.7 hectares) between Houston and Commerce Streets next to the Fort Worth Convention Center.

facts.fact: It was built in 1974 to a design by Philip Johnson and John Burgee and given to the city by the Amon G. Carter Foundation.
facts.quote: The Water Gardens were built in 1974, designed by noted New York architects Philip Johnson and John Burgee, and were dedicated to the City of Fort Worth by the Amon G. Carter Foundation.

facts.fact: Its focal points are three pools of water.
facts.quote: The focal points of the park are three pools of water.

facts.fact: In the Quiet Pool, thin sheets of water run down tall walls into a sunken pool ringed by cypress trees.
facts.quote: The Quiet Pool is encircled with cypress trees and towering walls that are covered in thin planes of water that cascade almost 90 degrees down to the sunken blue water feature.

facts.fact: In the Active Pool, water falls 38 ft (11 m) down terraces and steps into a small pool.
facts.quote: The Active Pool is the main attraction of the Water Gardens, and has water cascading 38 feet (11 m) down terraces and steps into a small pool at the bottom.

facts.fact: A terraced knoll shields the park from the rest of the city.
facts.quote: A terraced knoll helps to shield it from the rest of the City.

facts.fact: After four people drowned in 2004, the park reopened in 2007 with the main pool reduced from 9 ft to 2 ft deep.
facts.quote: The park reopened March 4, 2007, after modifications that reduced the depth of the main pool from 9 ft (2.7 m) to 2 ft (0.61 m) and addressed other issues.

facts.fact: Opened in 2003, the Nasher Sculpture Center in Dallas houses Patsy and Raymond Nasher's collection of modern and contemporary sculpture.
facts.quote: Opened in 2003, the Nasher Sculpture Center is a museum in Dallas, Texas, that houses the Patsy and Raymond Nasher collection of modern and contemporary sculpture.

facts.fact: It stands on a 2.4-acre site next to the Dallas Museum of Art in the Arts District.
facts.quote: It is located on a 2.4-acre (9,700 m2) site adjacent to the Dallas Museum of Art in the Dallas Arts District.

facts.fact: In 1997 Raymond Nasher bought the land and hired Renzo Piano to design the museum.
facts.quote: In 1997, Raymond Nasher acquired a plot of land in downtown Dallas across the street from the Dallas Museum of Art and hired architect Renzo Piano to design the Nasher Sculpture Center.

facts.fact: The Nasher Foundation paid the whole $70 million cost of the museum and its indoor and outdoor galleries.
facts.quote: The Nasher Foundation funded the entire $70 million cost of designing and constructing the museum, which includes indoor and outdoor galleries.

facts.fact: Piano worked with landscape architect Peter Walker of PWP Landscape Architecture on the 2-acre garden.
facts.quote: Piano worked in collaboration with landscape architect Peter Walker of PWP Landscape Architecture on the design of the 2-acre (8,100 m2) Garden.

facts.fact: Piano designed the roof to bring indirect sunlight into the galleries according to the sun's path, but glare from the glass Museum Tower now reaches them.
facts.quote: The Museum Tower's glass has reflected an undesirable glare into the nearby Nasher Sculpture Center, whose architect Renzo Piano had specifically designed its roof to direct appropriate indirect sunlight into the galleries, based on the arc of the sun across the sky.

facts.fact: The garden steps down to the auditorium, making an open-air theatre.
facts.quote: The garden terraces downward to the auditorium, creating an open-air theater.

facts.fact: The Beck Group built the building and acted as associate architect.
facts.quote: The building was constructed by The Beck Group, which also served as associate architect.

facts.fact: The Wyly Theatre is one of four venues of the AT&T Performing Arts Center in the Dallas Arts District, dedicated on 12 October 2009.
facts.quote: It is one of four venues that comprise the AT&T Performing Arts Center and was dedicated October 12, 2009.

facts.fact: The 80,300 sq ft building is twelve storeys tall and holds about 600 people, depending on the stage layout.
facts.quote: The 80,300-square-foot building is twelve stories tall and holds about 600 people, depending upon the stage configuration.

facts.fact: It was designed by REX | OMA, with Joshua Prince-Ramus as partner in charge and Rem Koolhaas.
facts.quote: The Wyly Theatre was designed by REX | OMA, Joshua Prince-Ramus (partner in charge) and Pritzker Prize winning architect Rem Koolhaas.

facts.fact: Its "stacked", vertically organised design rethinks the traditional form of a theatre.
facts.quote: It features a groundbreaking design with an unprecedented "stacked" vertically organized facility that completely rethinks the traditional form of theatre.

facts.fact: Vertical rods of extruded anodised aluminium on all four sides are meant to recall the folds of a theatre curtain.
facts.quote: The vertical rods lining the outside of the building on all four sides are intended to be symbolic of the folds of a theater curtain. The rods comprising the facade are extruded anodized aluminum.

facts.fact: It won an AIA National Honor Award in 2011.
facts.quote: 2011 AIA, National Honor Award (Dee and Charles Wyly Theatre)

facts.fact: It is the home of the Dallas Theater Center, Dallas Black Dance Theatre and Anita N. Martinez Ballet Folklorico.
facts.quote: It is the new venue for the Dallas Theater Center, Dallas Black Dance Theatre and Anita N. Martinez Ballet Folklorico.

facts.fact: The Oregon Convention Center in Portland was completed in 1989 and opened in 1990, east of the Willamette River.
facts.quote: Completed in 1989 and opened in 1990, it is located on the east side of the Willamette River in the Lloyd District neighborhood.

facts.fact: It is best known for its twin spire towers, which bring light inside, and for the world's largest Foucault pendulum.
facts.quote: It is best known for the twin spire towers, which provide light into the building's interior and for housing the world's largest Foucault pendulum.

facts.fact: It was designed by Zimmer Gunsul Frasca Architects (ZGF) and is Oregon's largest convention center, at nearly 1 million sq ft.
facts.quote: The building was designed by the architectural firm of Zimmer Gunsul Frasca Architects (ZGF). It is the largest convention center in Oregon, at nearly 1 million square feet (93,000 m2).

facts.fact: It was expanded in 2003, also with ZGF.
facts.quote: The original building was built in the late 1980s, opened in 1990, and was expanded in 2003. ZGF was also involved in designing the expansion.

facts.fact: It was the first existing convention center to get LEED Platinum.
facts.quote: It was the first existing one to receive the highest, platinum rating in the U.S. Green Building Council's LEED certification program and is the only one to have it for operations and maintenance.

facts.fact: A 6,500-panel solar array supplies about a quarter of its electricity.
facts.quote: A 6,500-panel solar array provides about 25 percent of the electricity used, and is the second largest one on a convention center in the country.

facts.fact: Public art by over two dozen mostly Pacific Northwest artists fills the building and grounds.
facts.quote: The building and grounds also have an extensive set of public art, with works from over two dozen mainly Pacific Northwest artists.

facts.fact: The museum was formerly the Pasadena Art Institute and Pasadena Art Museum.
facts.quote: It was previously known as the Pasadena Art Institute and the Pasadena Art Museum and displays numerous sculptures on its grounds.

facts.fact: Hopps insisted on a local architect because he expected close interaction throughout the design.
facts.quote: Hopps insisted on a local architect because he expected a high level of interaction throughout the design process.

facts.fact: The building was completed in 1969 to designs by Pasadena architects Thornton Ladd and John Kelsey (Ladd & Kelsey).
facts.quote: A new Pasadena Art Museum building was completed in 1969, designed by Pasadena architects Thornton Ladd and John Kelsey of the firm Ladd & Kelsey.

facts.fact: The curving facade is clad in 115,000 brown glazed tiles with an undulating surface, made by ceramicist Edith Heath.
facts.quote: The distinctive and modern curvilinear exterior facade is faced in 115,000 glazed tiles, in varying rich brown tones with an undulating surface, made by ceramic artisan Edith Heath.

facts.fact: It stands on Colorado Boulevard on the Rose Parade route, where its brown tile exterior appears on TV.
facts.quote: The museum is located on Colorado Boulevard along the route of the Tournament of Roses's Rose Parade, where its distinctive, brown tile exterior can be seen in the background of television broadcasts.

facts.fact: In 1995 Frank Gehry, a longtime trustee, began a $5 million renovation of the museum.
facts.quote: In 1995, the museum began a major $5 million renovation with the architect Frank Gehry, a longtime trustee of the museum.

facts.fact: The redesign made smaller galleries with raised ceilings and better lighting, a floor for Asian art and restored access to the gardens.
facts.quote: The redesign resulted in a procession of medium-size, more intimate galleries with raised ceilings and improved lighting, increased rotating exhibition space, an entire floor devoted to Asian art, and restored access to the gardens.

facts.fact: Jacobs Medical Center is a teaching hospital of UC San Diego Health, opened in 2016.
facts.quote: Jacobs Medical Center is a teaching hospital of UC San Diego Health at the University of California, San Diego. The facility was opened in 2016.

facts.fact: It is made of three specialty pavilions.
facts.quote: Jacobs Medical Center comprises three specialty pavilions.

facts.fact: Ground was broken on 9 April 2012.
facts.quote: The university broke ground on the new inpatient tower on April 9, 2012.

facts.fact: The 509,500 sq ft, 245-bed tower cost over $940 million, opened in November 2016 and was designed by CannonDesign.
facts.quote: The finished 509,500 sq ft, 245-bed tower cost more than $940 million and opened in November 2016. CannonDesign was the architect, Kitchell Contractors, Inc. was the general contractor.

facts.fact: First planned as a simple expansion of Thornton Hospital, it grew into a ten-storey quaternary care hospital.
facts.quote: The construction of Jacobs Medical Center was originally intended as a simple expansion of the hospital, but evolved into the ten-story quaternary care facility that exists today.

facts.fact: The hospital looks out over UC San Diego, the Torrey Pines Mesa, La Jolla and the Pacific Ocean.
facts.quote: The hospital has views of UC San Diego, the Torrey Pines Mesa, La Jolla and the Pacific Ocean.

facts.fact: The MacMillan Bloedel Building is a 27-storey Vancouver office tower built as the head office of the forestry company MacMillan Bloedel, designed by Erickson/Massey Architects.
facts.quote: The MacMillan Bloedel Building is a 27-storey office tower in Vancouver, British Columbia. The building was constructed as the head office of the forestry company MacMillan Bloedel and was designed by Erickson/Massey Architects.

facts.fact: Arthur Erickson conceived it in 1965; construction began in October 1966 and it opened on 13 December 1968.
facts.quote: The partner-in-charge of design was Arthur Erickson, who conceived the building in 1965. Construction began in October 1966 and the building opened officially on 13 December 1968.

facts.fact: It is one of Erickson's earliest works and one of Canada's outstanding examples of brutalist architecture.
facts.quote: The building is one of the earliest works in Erickson's catalogue and is one of Canada's outstanding examples of brutalist architecture.

facts.fact: It is two parallel, offset towers joined by a mechanical core.
facts.quote: Erickson's design consists of two parallel off-set towers connected by a mechanical core.

facts.fact: Load-bearing concrete outer walls leave the floors column-free, and they taper from ten feet thick at the base to one foot at the top.
facts.quote: The building has load-bearing concrete exterior walls that create a column-free floor plate. Walls taper in thickness from ten feet at the base to one foot at the top.

facts.fact: The 7 by 7 ft windows are single panes set straight into the concrete wall.
facts.quote: The 7' by 7' windows are set into the concrete wall and are single panes of glass.

facts.fact: Erickson called it "a Doric building in its starkness and simplicity".
facts.quote: Erickson characterised his work as "a Doric building in its starkness and simplicity."

facts.fact: It won the Massey Medal for Architecture in 1970.
facts.quote: In 1970, the MacMillan Bloedel Building won the Massey Medal for Architecture.

facts.fact: The Lester B. Pearson Building at 125 Sussex Drive, Ottawa, is the headquarters of Global Affairs Canada.
facts.quote: It is located at 125 Sussex Drive in the Lower Town neighbourhood and currently serves as the headquarters of Global Affairs Canada.

facts.fact: Queen Elizabeth II officially opened it on 1 August 1973.
facts.quote: It was officially opened on 1 August 1973 by Queen Elizabeth II.

facts.fact: It was designed by the Toronto firm Webb Zerafa Menkes and is described as late modern with an influence of Brutalism.
facts.quote: The building was designed by the Toronto-based architectural firm of Webb Zerafa Menkes and is described as "late modern with an influence of Brutalism".

facts.fact: It is made of four towers of 4 to 10 storeys, three of them linked from the first to the fifth floor.
facts.quote: The building consists of four "towers" ranging from 4 to 10 storeys, of which three are interconnected from the first to the fifth floor.

facts.fact: In 2013 it was designated a Federal Heritage Building.
facts.quote: In 2013, the Department of Public Works and Government Services designated the office complex a Federal Heritage Building for its "historical associations, and its architectural and environmental values".

facts.fact: A renovation begun in 2019, estimated at $700 million, is due to finish in 2028.
facts.quote: The project is estimated to cost $700 million and is scheduled to be completed in 2028.

facts.fact: Théâtre Maisonneuve is a theatre at Place des Arts in Montreal's Quartier des spectacles.
facts.quote: It is located at Place des Arts in the Quartier des spectacles neighbourhood in the borough of Ville-Marie.

facts.fact: It opened in 1967 and is named after Paul Chomedey de Maisonneuve, the founder of Montreal.
facts.quote: Théâtre Maisonneuve was inaugurated in 1967 and was named for the founder of Montreal, Paul Chomedey de Maisonneuve.

facts.fact: It has 1,453 seats and hosts variety shows, small ensembles, soloists, musicals and films.
facts.quote: The theatre has 1,453 seats and is used for variety shows, benefits small ensembles and soloists, musicals and films.

facts.fact: Montreal architects Pierre Boulva and Jacques David designed Théâtre Maisonneuve among their other city projects.
facts.quote: It was designed by Montreal architects Pierre Boulva and Jacques David, whose other prominent Montreal projects included the Palais de justice de Montréal, Théâtre Maisonneuve, the Dow Planetarium and the Place-des-Arts, Atwater and Lucien-L'Allier metro stations.

facts.fact: Roy Thomson Hall is a Toronto concert hall, home to the Toronto Symphony Orchestra and the Toronto Mendelssohn Choir.
facts.quote: Located downtown in the city's entertainment district, it is home to the Toronto Symphony Orchestra, the Toronto Mendelssohn Choir, and the esports team Toronto Defiant.

facts.fact: Opened in 1982, it is circular, with a sloping, curving glass exterior.
facts.quote: Opened in 1982, its circular architectural design exhibits a sloping and curvilinear glass exterior.

facts.fact: It was designed by Arthur Erickson and Mathers and Haldenby, with Itzhak Perlman advising on access for disabled performers and guests.
facts.quote: It was designed by Canadian architects Arthur Erickson and Mathers and Haldenby. Itzhak Perlman acted as a special advisor to the architects on accessibility needs for disabled performers and guests.

facts.fact: It was built between 1972 and 1982.
facts.quote: Roy Thomson Hall was built between 1972 and 1982, and was designed by Erickson with the assistance of the Toronto firm of Mathers and Haldenby.

facts.fact: The hall seats 2,630 and has a pipe organ by Gabriel Kney.
facts.quote: The hall seats 2,630 guests and features a pipe organ built by Canadian organ builder Gabriel Kney from London, Ontario.

facts.fact: Erickson saw the grey building as a container for people to fill with their own decorations.
facts.quote: Erickson speaks of the point of the grey structure being that of a container which people were to fill up with their own decorations.

facts.fact: The design was influenced by Erickson's travels in Japan and his relationship with North American Aboriginal peoples.
facts.quote: The building was influenced by Erickson's journeys in Japan and his relationship with the North American Aboriginals.

facts.fact: It was renovated over six months in 2002 after years of complaints about its acoustics.
facts.quote: The hall was renovated over a period of six months in 2002, after years of complaints from musicians about the quality of its acoustics.

facts.fact: The Grande Bibliothèque is a public library in downtown Montreal, part of Quebec's national library (BAnQ).
facts.quote: The Grande Bibliothèque (French pronunciation: [ɡʁɑ̃d biblijɔtɛk]) is a public library in Downtown Montreal, Quebec, Canada. Its collection is part of Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec (BAnQ), Quebec's national library.

facts.fact: It was designed by Patkau Architects of Vancouver with Croft-Pelletier/Gilles Guité of Quebec City.
facts.quote: The Grande Bibliothèque, which had been a pet project of former Québec premier Lucien Bouchard, was designed by Patkau Architects from Vancouver and Croft-Pelletier/Gilles Guité from Quebec City.

facts.fact: Construction of the 33,000 m² library, a $90.6 million project, began in 2001 on the site of the former Palais du commerce.
facts.quote: Construction on the new 33,000 m2 library, a $90.6 million project began in 2001 on the site of the former Palais du commerce.

facts.fact: The five-storey building is clad in horizontal U-shaped glass plates, a type never used before in North America, on full-height copper uprights.
facts.quote: The contemporary-styled five-storey building is clad with U-shaped plates of glass of a type never used before in North America, placed horizontally on the copper uprights that run the whole height of the building.

facts.fact: Multi-storey reading areas are walled in slats of Québec yellow birch that let in or block indirect daylight as the collection needs.
facts.quote: These multi-storey areas are demarcated by walls of wooden slats, either allowing indirect natural light or blocking it according to the conservation needs of the collection. The slats are made of Québec-grown yellow birch, the official tree of Québec.

facts.fact: It is linked directly by the underground city to Berri–UQAM metro station.
facts.quote: It is connected directly by the underground city to Berri–UQAM station, a factor cited by the institution for its success.

facts.fact: In 2011 it drew 2.7 million visitors, the most of any public library in North America and the Francophonie.
facts.quote: In 2011, it attracted 2.7 million visitors, and was the most frequented public library in both North America and the Francophonie.

facts.fact: Our Lady of Victory, the Igloo Church, is a Catholic church in downtown Inuvik, Northwest Territories, opened and consecrated in 1960 after two years of building.
facts.quote: It was established in the mid-1950s, around the time Inuvik was being built; the church was opened and consecrated in 1960 after two years of construction.

facts.fact: It was designed by Brother Maurice Larocque, a missionary and former carpenter with no formal architectural training, who sketched it on two sheets of plywood.
facts.quote: Brother Maurice Larocque, a Catholic missionary to the Arctic who had previously been a carpenter, designed the church despite a lack of any formal architectural training, sketching it on two sheets of plywood that are prominently displayed in the building's upper storeys.

facts.fact: The round, igloo-painted shape was chosen to limit damage from frost heave.
facts.quote: The round shape, which is painted to mimic an igloo, was chosen to mitigate possible structural damage that might be caused by frost heave.

facts.fact: Its "dome within a dome" rests on a bowl-shaped concrete slab on gravel over the permafrost, with wooden arches carrying the load.
facts.quote: Its unique structural system, "a dome within a dome", further protects the church with a foundation consisting of a bowl-shaped concrete slab on a gravel bed atop the permafrost and, in the building itself, an intricate system of wooden arches to support the load.

facts.fact: It is the only major building in Inuvik not on pilings, and its wood was floated nearly 2,000 km down the Mackenzie River.
facts.quote: It is the only major building in Inuvik that does not rest on pilings. Wood for the church was floated down the Mackenzie River from Fort Smith, nearly 2,000 kilometres (1,200 mi) away.

facts.fact: It is a circular timber-frame building 23 m (75 ft) across.
facts.quote: The church building itself is a circular timber frame structure 23 metres (75 ft) in diameter on a foundation of a reinforced concrete basement on a bowl-shaped concrete slab that itself sits on a metre-thick (3 ft) gravel bed atop the permafrost that is generally found at 2 metres (6 ft) underground at Inuvik's latitude.

facts.fact: The domed roof is covered in diamond-shaped aluminium scales, with a 6.1 m cupola at its centre.
facts.quote: The domed roof is sheathed in diamond-shaped aluminum scales. Ribs delineate each of the building's bays. At the centre of the dome is a round 6.1-metre-wide (20 ft) cupola, set with very narrow stained glass windows divided by projecting wooden strips.

facts.fact: The 12 main laminated wooden vaults meet at a central rosette under the cupola, ringed by small windows that let in daylight.
facts.quote: They meet at a central rosette below the cupola, bordered by small windows that let natural light in.

facts.fact: The Peace Bridge carries people walking and cycling across the Bow River in Calgary; Santiago Calatrava designed it and it opened on 24 March 2012.
facts.quote: Peace Bridge is a bridge that accommodates people walking and cycling across the Bow River in Calgary, Alberta, Canada. The bridge was designed by Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava and opened on March 24, 2012.

facts.fact: It links downtown and the south pathway with the north pathway and the Sunnyside community.
facts.quote: The City of Calgary built the bridge to connect the southern Bow River pathway and Downtown Calgary with the northern Bow River pathway and the community of Sunnyside.

facts.fact: The brief allowed no piers in the water and limited the height because of a nearby heliport.
facts.quote: The design follows strict requirements with no piers in the water (in an effort to minimize the ecological footprint) and restricted height (due to the vicinity of the City/Bow River Heliport).

facts.fact: Unlike Calatrava's usual asymmetric, high-masted, white bridges, it is red and white, the colours of the Canadian and Calgary flags.
facts.quote: The bridge is a departure from Calatrava's previous designs, which were typically asymmetric shapes anchored by high masts. Another atypical element is the color; while most of Calatrava's designs are white, the Peace Bridge features red and white as used in both the flag of Canada and the flag of Calgary.

facts.fact: The tubular bridge was made in Spain, shipped to Calgary, and moved across the river in November 2011.
facts.quote: The tubular bridge was manufactured in Spain and shipped to Calgary.  Assembly of the bridge pieces started in Fall 2010 and the bridge was moved across the Bow River in November 2011.

facts.fact: It is a helical steel tube of 850 tonnes with a glass roof.
facts.quote: Helical steel structure with a glass roof (850-tonne steel)

facts.fact: After vandalism to its glass panels in 2022, the city and Calatrava chose to replace them with steel cables.
facts.quote: In order to reduce the cost of replacing the glass, the city consulted with Calatrava and decided to install steel cables instead, to be completed in fall 2023.

facts.fact: The Monumento a la Revolución is a memorial arch to the Mexican Revolution in the Plaza de la República, Mexico City.
facts.quote: The Monument to the Revolution (Spanish: Monumento a la Revolución) is a memorial arch commemorating the Mexican Revolution. It is located in the Plaza de la República, near the heart of the major thoroughfares Paseo de la Reforma and Avenida de los Insurgentes in downtown Mexico City.

facts.fact: At 67 m (220 ft) it is the tallest triumphal arch in the world.
facts.quote: It is the tallest triumphal arch in the world, standing 67 m (220 ft) high.

facts.fact: It began as the Federal Legislative Palace under Porfirio Díaz, left unfinished because of the Revolution.
facts.quote: The building would hold the congressional chambers of the deputies and senators, but the project was not finished due to the Mexican Revolution.

facts.fact: French architect Émile Bénard designed the palace in a neoclassical style with French Renaissance touches.
facts.quote: Porfirio Díaz appointed a French architect, Émile Bénard to design and construct the structure, a neoclassical design with "characteristic touches of the French renaissance," showing government officials' aim to demonstrate Mexico's rightful place as an advanced nation.

facts.fact: The inner structure was iron, with a facade planned in Italian marble and Norwegian granite.
facts.quote: The internal structure was made of iron, and rather than using local Mexican materials in the stone façade, the design called for Italian marble and Norwegian granite.

facts.fact: Under Lázaro Cárdenas, architect Carlos Obregón Santacilia proposed turning the abandoned dome shell into a monument to the heroes of the Revolution.
facts.quote: The structure remained unfinished for twenty-five years, until the presidency of Lázaro Cárdenas, when Mexican architect Carlos Obregón Santacilia proposed converting the abandoned shell of the dome into a monument to the heroes of the Mexican Revolution.

facts.fact: The conversion was built over the existing cupola in an eclectic Art Deco and Mexican socialist realist style.
facts.quote: After this was approved, the structure began its eclectic Art Deco and Mexican socialist realism conversion, building over the existing cupola structure.

facts.fact: Sculptor Oliverio Martínez designed its four stone sculpture groups, and work was completed in 1938.
facts.quote: Mexican sculptor Oliverio Martínez designed four stone sculpture groups for the monument, with Francisco Zúñiga as one of his assistants. Work was completed in 1938.

facts.fact: It is also a mausoleum for leading figures of the Revolution.
facts.quote: The structure also functions as a mausoleum for some of the key figures of the Mexican Revolution of 1910, namely Francisco I. Madero, Francisco "Pancho" Villa, Venustiano Carranza, Plutarco Elías Calles, and Lázaro Cárdenas.

facts.fact: The Torre del Reformador is a 71.85 m (236 ft) steel framework tower in Zone 9 of Guatemala City.
facts.quote: The Torre del Reformador (Tower of the Reformer) is a 71.85 meter (236 ft.) tall steel framework tower in Zone 9 of Guatemala City.

facts.fact: It was built in 1935 for the 100th anniversary of the birth of President Justo Rufino Barrios, a reformer.
facts.quote: The tower was built in 1935, to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the birth of Justo Rufino Barrios, who was President of Guatemala and instituted a number of reforms.

facts.fact: Its basic shape resembles the Eiffel Tower; the bell at its top was replaced by a beacon in 1986.
facts.quote: The basic shape of the structure resembles the Eiffel Tower. It was originally constructed with a bell on its top, which in 1986 was replaced with a beacon.

facts.fact: It was made in the United States of galvanised iron and assembled by engineer Arturo Bickford, then mayor of the city.
facts.quote: The Tower of the Reformer was constructed in the United States, with galvanized iron, to a cost of Q49,775.60 and was assembled by the Engineer Arturo Bickford, Mayor of the City at that time.

facts.fact: It was fabricated by the United States Steel Products Company.
facts.quote: The tower had been fabricated by the United States Steel Products Company.

facts.fact: It was inaugurated on 19 July 1935 by General Jorge Ubico Castañeda.
facts.quote: With a height of 71.85 meters, the Commemorative Tower of the 19 of the July (later renamed Tower of the Reformer) was inaugurated on the 19 of July 1935 by General Jorge Ubico Castañeda, in commemoration of the one hundredth anniversary of the birth of  General Justo Rufino Barrios.

facts.fact: The tower was first lit electrically on 26 September 1958.
facts.quote: The first electric illumination of the tower happened on 26 September 1958 and was financed by the brewery company Cervecería Centro Americana.

facts.fact: The Hotel Nacional de Cuba is a Spanish eclectic hotel in Havana, opened in 1930 on Taganana Hill on the Vedado sea front.
facts.quote: The Hotel Nacional de Cuba is a historic Spanish eclectic style hotel in Havana, Cuba, opened in 1930. Located on the sea front of Vedado district, it stands on Taganana Hill, offering commanding views of the sea and the city.

facts.fact: McKim, Mead and White designed it, and Purdy and Henderson built it in fourteen months.
facts.quote: The Hotel Nacional was designed by the New York architecture firm of McKim, Mead and White, financed by the National City Bank of New York, and constructed in fourteen months by the U.S. engineering firm of Purdy and Henderson.

facts.fact: It mixes Sevillian, Roman, Moorish and Art Deco styles, with a Palladian entrance portico in coral stone.
facts.quote: The structure contains a mix of styles, including Sevillian, Roman, Moorish and Art Deco. The Palladian style entrance portico has two stylized column capitals and quoins of coral stone.

facts.fact: The plan is based on two Greek crosses, giving most rooms an ocean view.
facts.quote: The layout of the Hotel Nacional is based on two Greek crosses, giving the majority of the rooms a view of the ocean.

facts.fact: It has a steel frame, with much of its decoration, columns and paving in coral stone.
facts.quote: The structure of the building is a steel frame, while the decorative elements including ground floor details, columns, wall facings, and much of the paving, are in coral stone.

facts.fact: It opened on 30 December 1930.
facts.quote: The hotel opened as The National Hotel of Cuba on December 30, 1930, operated by the American managers of the Plaza Hotel, Savoy-Plaza Hotel and Copley Plaza Hotel, at a time when Cuba was a prime travel destination for people in the U.S.

facts.fact: In 1933 it was the scene of a bloody siege, the Battle of the Hotel Nacional.
facts.quote: Soon after, on October 2, 1933, it was the site of a bloody siege that would become known as the Battle of the Hotel Nacional of Cuba.

facts.fact: During the Cuban Missile Crisis, anti-aircraft guns and tunnels were built on the site; the tunnels are now open to visitors.
facts.quote: During the Cuban Missile Crisis, anti-aircraft guns were set up on the site of the Santa Clara Battery and an extensive series of tunnels were built under the property, which are now open to the public on guided tours.

facts.fact: The Gran Teatro de La Habana is a theatre in Havana and home to the Cuban National Ballet.
facts.quote: Gran Teatro de La Habana is a theater in Havana, Cuba, home to the Cuban National Ballet.

facts.fact: Belgian architect Paul Belau designed it, and Purdy and Henderson built it in 1914 on the site of the former Teatro Tacón.
facts.quote: It was designed by the Belgian architect Paul Belau and built by Purdy and Henderson, Engineers in 1914 at the site of the former Teatro Tacón.

facts.fact: Havana's Galician immigrants paid for it as a community and social centre.
facts.quote: Its construction was paid for by the Galician immigrants of Havana to serve as a community-social center.

facts.fact: The Baroque Revival Centro Gallego was built around the old Teatro Tacón concert hall, enlarging its support spaces and adding an elaborate system of circulation.
facts.quote: Architect Paul Belau, architect of the Presidential Palace, and the U.S. firm Purdy and Henderson, Engineers, kept the original theatre and built the Centro Gallego, a Baroque Revival style building addition that enlarged the support functions of the concert hall and introduced an elaborate system of circulation.

facts.fact: The old Teatro Tacón exterior got new stone facing to match the Centro Gallego.
facts.quote: The exterior of the original Teatro Tacón received a new stone facing to harmonize with the new exterior of the Centro Gallego.

facts.fact: Four white marble sculptures by Giuseppe Moretti and Geneva Mercer represent charity, education, music and theatre.
facts.quote: There is a group of four sculptures in white marble, part of a group of ninety-seven, by Giuseppe Moretti and Geneva Mercer representing charity, education, music and theater.

facts.fact: Its main hall, the García Lorca Auditorium, seats 1,500.
facts.quote: Currently, the principal venue is the García Lorca Auditorium, with seats for 1,500 persons, it provides a home for the Cuban National Ballet Company, and for other dance companies and musical performances.

facts.fact: It has hosted the International Ballet Festival of Havana every two years since 1960.
facts.quote: It hosts the International Ballet Festival of Havana every two years since 1960.

facts.fact: Saint Joseph's Oratory is a National Historic Site of Canada and Canada's largest church, with one of the world's largest church domes.
facts.quote: It is a National Historic Site of Canada and is Canada's largest church, with one of the largest church domes in the world.

facts.fact: Founded in 1904 by Saint André Bessette, it was built by many architects and thousands of workers over six decades.
facts.quote: Founded in 1904 by Saint André Bessette in honour of his patron saint, Saint Joseph, the Oratory is the product of numerous architects and thousands of workers in a process spanning six decades.

facts.fact: It has a Renaissance Revival facade and a contrasting Art Deco interior.
facts.quote: With its monumental scale, Renaissance Revival facade and contrasting Art Deco interior, the Oratory is recognizable not just in Montreal but around the world, attracting more than 2 million visitors and pilgrims to its steps each year.

facts.fact: It is Montreal's highest building, rising more than 30 m above the summit of Mount Royal.
facts.quote: The Oratory is the highest building in Montreal, rising more than 30 metres above Mount Royal's summit, allowing it to be seen from many kilometres away.

facts.fact: Dalbé Viau and Alphonse Venne built the 1,000-seat crypt church from 1914 to 1916.
facts.quote: From 1914 to 1916, Viau and Venne constructed the crypt church, with seating for 1,000, which still stands today and forms the base of the basilica where the massive collection of stairs ends.

facts.fact: From 1937 Dom Paul Bellot, working through Lucien Parent, redesigned the dome much larger, modelled on Florence Cathedral.
facts.quote: He redesigned Viau and Venne's roof and dome entirely, making the dome significantly larger and modelling it to resemble the dome of Florence Cathedral. The construction of his large Oratory dome lasted four years and was completed in 1941 after involving thousands of workers.

facts.fact: The outer dome is 39 m across and rises 97 m above the nave floor; the inner dome is 26 m across.
facts.quote: The two domes vary immensely in span and height, with the outer dome measuring 39 m (128 ft) in diameter and rising 97 m (318 ft) from the nave floor, and the inner dome measuring 26 m (85 ft) in diameter and rising 60 m (200 ft) from the nave floor.

facts.fact: At the summer solstice the setting sun lines up with the main steps, the aisle and the altar cross.
facts.quote: During the summer solstice, the setting sun is perfectly aligned with the center line of the main steps that lead up to (and into) the basilica.

facts.fact: Old City Hall is a Romanesque civic building in Toronto, home of the city council from 1899 to 1966 and a court house until 2023.
facts.quote: The Old City Hall is a Romanesque-style civic building and former court house in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. It was the home of the Toronto City Council from 1899 to 1966 and a provincial court house until 2023, and remains one of the city's most prominent structures.

facts.fact: On completion in 1899 it was the largest civic building in North America.
facts.quote: Toronto's Old City Hall was one of the largest buildings in Toronto and the largest civic building in North America upon completion in 1899.

facts.fact: Designed by E. J. Lennox, it took more than a decade to build and cost more than $2.5 million.
facts.quote: Designed by prominent Toronto architect Edward James Lennox, the building took more than a decade to build and cost more than $2.5 million (equals close to 53 million today).

facts.fact: It is built of Credit River sandstone, grey Orangeville stone and brown New Brunswick stone.
facts.quote: It was constructed of sandstone from the Credit River valley, grey stone from the Orangeville, Ontario, area, and brown stone from New Brunswick.

facts.fact: Refused a plaque, Lennox had his name carved in the corbels under the eaves around the whole building.
facts.quote: Not to be denied, Lennox had stonemasons "sign" his name in corbels beneath the upper floor eaves around the entire building: "EJ LENNOX ARCHITECT AD 1898".

facts.fact: It is a large square block around a courtyard, with the clock tower set off-centre to close the view up Bay Street.
facts.quote: Old City Hall can be described as an enormous square quad with a courtyard in the middle. Situated at the front elevation, its clock tower was placed off centre to provide a terminating vista for Bay Street.

facts.fact: Lennox designed it in Richardsonian Romanesque, a variation of Romanesque Revival.
facts.quote: Old City Hall was designed by architect E. J. Lennox in a variation of Romanesque Revival architecture known as Richardsonian Romanesque.

facts.fact: It was designated a National Historic Site in 1984.
facts.quote: Old City Hall was designated a National Historic Site in 1984.

facts.fact: The Davis Building is the oldest and largest building on the University of Toronto's Mississauga campus.
facts.quote: The William G. Davis Building (commonly known as the Davis Building) is an academic building of the University of Toronto and the oldest and largest structure on its Mississauga campus in Mississauga, Ontario, Canada.

facts.fact: Raymond Moriyama designed it as a single mega-structure above the Credit River valley for the new Erindale College.
facts.quote: The building was part of the initial plans for Erindale College, designed by architect Raymond Moriyama to be a single mega-structure atop the valley of the Credit River.

facts.fact: Completed in 1973 as the South Building, the brutalist structure is still the campus's largest academic space.
facts.quote: Completed in 1973 as the South Building, the brutalist structure remains the largest academic space on the campus.

facts.fact: Moriyama's plan put all academic facilities in one central building to preserve the campus's natural setting.
facts.quote: Moriyama's approved plan envisioned one central building that would hold all academic facilities, thus preserving the campus's natural state.

facts.fact: Moriyama took the project over from John Andrews; it was one of his first major commissions.
facts.quote: For unknown reasons, architect Raymond Moriyama took over the project and created a new design, becoming one of his first major commissions.

facts.fact: It is built mainly of exposed concrete on the west bank of the Credit River.
facts.quote: It was constructed on the west bank of the Credit River, north of Wilson Pond, primarily out of exposed concrete in a style characterized as brutalist architecture.

facts.fact: It was renamed in 2010 for William G. Davis, Ontario's education minister and premier.
facts.quote: It was given its present name in honour of Ontario premier and education minister William G. Davis in 2010.

facts.fact: The Plaza de las Tres Culturas is the main square of the Tlatelolco neighbourhood in Mexico City.
facts.quote: The Plaza de las Tres Culturas ("The Three Cultures square") is the main square within the Tlatelolco neighborhood of Mexico City.

facts.fact: Its name refers to three periods of Mexican history seen in its buildings: pre-Columbian, Spanish colonial and the independent nation.
facts.quote: The name "Three Cultures" is in recognition of the three periods of Mexican history reflected by buildings in the square: pre-Columbian, Spanish colonial, and the independent nation.

facts.fact: Mexican architect and urbanist Mario Pani designed the square, completed in 1966.
facts.quote: The square, designed by Mexican architect and urbanist Mario Pani, was completed in 1966.

facts.fact: It holds the archaeological site of Tlatelolco and is flanked by the 1536 College of Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco and a large 1964 housing complex.
facts.quote: The square contains the archaeological site of the city-state of Tlatelolco and is flanked by the oldest European school of higher learning in the Americas called the College of Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco (built in 1536 by friar Juan de Torquemada) and by a massive housing complex built in 1964.

facts.fact: The Nonoalco-Tlatelolco housing complex surrounds the plaza, which symbolises the synthesis of Mexico's pre-Hispanic and colonial past with the present.
facts.quote: It surrounds the Plaza de las Tres Culturas, a place that symbolizes the synthesis of Mexico's pre-Hispanic  and colonial pasts with the modern day.

facts.fact: The Tlatelolco massacre of 2 October 1968 took place on the plaza.
facts.quote: Quality of life in the area diminished after the Tlatelolco massacre on 2 October 1968, which occurred on the Plaza de las Tres Culturas.

facts.fact: The former foreign ministry building on its south edge now houses Memorial 68, a museum opened in 2007.
facts.quote: This headquarters now houses a memorial museum called "Memorial 68", opened by UNAM in October 2007, to remember the 1968 Mexican student demonstrations and the Tlatelolco Massacre victims and survivors.

facts.fact: The National Theatre of Panama stands in Panama's old city, next to the church of San Francisco and the Plaza Bolívar.
facts.quote: The National Theatre of Panama (Spanish: Teatro Nacional de Panamá) is located in the old city of Panama, next to the church of San Francisco and the Plaza Bolívar.

facts.fact: Its construction was ordered by Act 52 of 1904.
facts.quote: Its construction was ordered by Act 52 of 1904.

facts.fact: The theatre is part of a cross-shaped building, with ceiling frescoes by Panamanian painter Roberto Lewis.
facts.quote: The National Theatre is part of a cross-shaped building. Ceiling frescos were done by famed Panamanian Robert Lewis.

facts.fact: Italian architect Genaro Ruggieri designed it in the style of an Italian operetta theatre; it opened on 1 October 1908.
facts.quote: The theater was designed by Italian architect Genaro Ruggieri, with a style of Italian operetta theater, and opened on October 1, 1908.

facts.fact: Ruggieri's neoclassical architecture was the official architecture of the time, seen in the National Theatre and other public buildings.
facts.quote: The neoclassical architecture introduced by Genaro Ruggieri was the “official architecture” of the time and is reflected in works such as the National Theatre, the Palacio de las Garzas (Presidential Palace), the Palace of Justice, the Municipal Palace and the National Institute.

facts.fact: Lewis's main curtain, ceiling painting and foyer date from 1907.
facts.quote: From that period (1907) date the main curtain, the ceiling painting and the foyer of the National Theatre of Panama.

facts.fact: The Groninger Museum is an art museum in Groningen showing modern and contemporary art.
facts.quote: The Groninger Museum (Dutch pronunciation: [ˈɣroːnɪŋər myˈzeːjʏm]) is an art museum in the city of Groningen in the Netherlands. The museum exhibits modern and contemporary art of local, national, and international artists.

facts.fact: Its post-modernist building of three main pavilions by Philippe Starck, Alessandro Mendini and Coop Himmelb(l)au was completed in 1994.
facts.quote: The current post-modernist building consists of three main pavilions designed individually by architects Philippe Starck, Alessandro Mendini, Coop Himmelb(l)au, and was completed in 1994.

facts.fact: The buildings stand in a canal opposite Groningen railway station: a silver cylinder by Starck, a yellow tower by Mendini and a pale blue deconstructivist space by Coop Himmelb(l)au.
facts.quote: The postmodernist structures that form the Groninger Museum stand in a canal opposite Groningen railway station. They consist of three main pavilions: a silver cylindrical building designed by Philippe Starck, a yellow tower by Alessandro Mendini, and a pale blue deconstructivist space by Coop Himmelb(l)au.

facts.fact: A bridge links the museum to the station as part of a cycling and walking path into the city centre.
facts.quote: A bridge that connects the museum to the train station is part of a cycling and walking path to the centre of the city.

facts.fact: Its colourful, futuristic style echoes the Memphis Group's Italian Post Modern designs.
facts.quote: The architecture's futuristic and colourful style echoes the Italian Post Modern designs of the Memphis Group.

facts.fact: Artist Frank Stella was first asked to design one pavilion, but his plan to build it entirely of Teflon proved too expensive.
facts.quote: American artist Frank Stella was originally approached to design one of the pavilions. However, his plan turned-out to be too expensive because he wanted his structure completely built out of Teflon.

facts.fact: Gasunie granted 25 million guilders for the new building.
facts.quote: Gasunie agreed to Hak's proposal and granted 25 million guilders for the project.

facts.fact: It is considered one of the most remarkable postmodern buildings of the late 20th century.
facts.quote: Especially, The Groninger Museum is considered one of the most amazing postmodern buildings of the late 20th century, and was also selected as one of the “1001 Buildings You Must See Before You Die.”

facts.fact: Ben van Berkel and his studio designed the Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam.
facts.quote: With his studio he designed, among others, the Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam, the Moebius House in the Netherlands, the Mercedes-Benz Museum in Stuttgart, Germany, Arnhem Central Station, the Singapore University of Architecture and Design, Raffles City in Hangzhou and numerous other buildings.

facts.fact: The bridge was realised by Van Berkel & Bos Architectuurbureau, the Amsterdam practice he set up with Caroline Bos in 1988.
facts.quote: In 1988 he and Caroline Bos set up an architectural practice in Amsterdam named Van Berkel & Bos Architectuurbureau, which realized, amongst other projects, the Karbouw office building and the Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam.

facts.fact: The project ran from 1991 to 1996.
facts.quote: Erasmus Bridge (1991–1996), Rotterdam, Netherlands

facts.fact: Het Nieuwe Instituut is a Rotterdam cultural centre for architecture, design and digital culture.
facts.quote: Nieuwe Instituut (NI, English: New Institute) is a cultural centre in Rotterdam, the Netherlands. It focuses on architecture, design, and digital culture.

facts.fact: It occupies a building by Jo Coenen at Museumpark 25, next to Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen.
facts.quote: NI is in a building designed by Jo Coenen at Museumpark 25 in the centre of Rotterdam, adjacent to the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen.

facts.fact: Coenen designed it as the Netherlands Architecture Institute between 1988 and 1993.
facts.quote: Other larger projects designed by Coenen include The Dutch Architecture Institute (originally called the Het Nieuwe Instituut) in the Museumpark of Rotterdam (1988–1993), the Smalle Haven area in Eindhoven (which includes the construction of the Vestedatoren, 2000–2006) en the Innovatoren in Venlo (2009-2011).

facts.fact: The building was opened by Queen Beatrix in 1993; in 2013 the Dutch institutes for architecture, design and digital culture were merged into it.
facts.quote: Thus the Netherlands Architecture Institute, Premsela Dutch Platform for Design and Fashion, and the Virtueel Platform were put together in the building at Museum Park 25, which was designed by Jo Coenen, and opened by Queen Beatrix in 1993.

facts.fact: It holds the national collection for Dutch architecture and urban planning.
facts.quote: The building also contains the national collection for Dutch architecture and urban planning, an agency, a study centre, a bookshop and a cafe.

facts.fact: Its archive holds over 18 km of architectural material, including many Dutch architects' personal collections.
facts.quote: The archive contains over 18 kilometres of architectural resources. This includes the personal collections of many Dutch architects.

facts.fact: The complex includes a pond, a small park and the Sonneveld House, a prime example of Nieuwe Zakelijkheid architecture.
facts.quote: The building contains a shop, exhibition space, study centre, and archive, as well as the Sonneveld House (a prime example of Nieuwe Zakelijkheid architecture), a pond, and a small park.

facts.fact: The Timmerhuis in central Rotterdam combines post-war reconstruction architecture by J.R.A. Koops with new architecture by OMA.
facts.quote: The building is a combination of post-World War II reconstruction architecture by municipal architect J.R.A. Koops and contemporary architecture by the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA).

facts.fact: Koops's L-shaped office building, built 1950–1953, was one of the first large buildings in Rotterdam's bombed centre.
facts.quote: Its construction took place between 1950 and 1953; it was one of the first larger buildings in the empty center of Rotterdam to be erected after the bombing.

facts.fact: Its gabled roofs look traditional, but its concrete skeleton, flexible ventilation and self-service lifts were progressive.
facts.quote: It features gabled roofs and chimneys, giving it a traditionalist look, but it was also considered progressive, due to the concrete skeleton, flexible ventilation system and self-service elevators.

facts.fact: OMA's winning design is a set of white glass cubes cantilevered over a steel structure on two legs.
facts.quote: It is a set of white glass cubes, cantilevered over a steel construction on two legs.

facts.fact: The new Timmerhuis opened on 11 December 2015 with offices, 91 apartments, parking and Museum Rotterdam.
facts.quote: The new complex, the Timmerhuis, opened on December 11, 2015. It contains offices, 91 apartments, an underground parking garage and houses Museum Rotterdam.

facts.fact: The extension has two towers of stepped residential floors with roof terraces, and a public passage through the atrium between them.
facts.quote: The extension comprises two towers, consisting of step-shaped, receding residential floors with roof terraces. On the ground floor, between the towers, is an atrium with a publicly accessible pedestrian passage (Halvemaanpassage) that connects Haagseveer with Rodezand.

facts.fact: The 1953 building became a municipal heritage monument in 2000.
facts.quote: In 2000, the building received the status of a municipal heritage monument and has been extensively restored.

facts.fact: The Royal Palace on Dam Square is one of three palaces at the Dutch monarch's disposal.
facts.quote: The Royal Palace of Amsterdam in Amsterdam (Dutch: Koninklijk Paleis van Amsterdam or Paleis op de Dam) is one of three palaces in the Netherlands which are at the disposal of the monarch by Act of Parliament.

facts.fact: It was built in the mid-17th century as Amsterdam's city hall and became a royal palace in 1808.
facts.quote: The palace was originally built in the mid-seventeenth century as the new city hall for the city of Amsterdam, and only became a royal palace in 1808 when the Netherlands were part of the First French Republic and First Empire under Napoleon Bonaparte.

facts.fact: The city hall opened on 29 July 1655.
facts.quote: The new stadhuis (City hall) was opened on 29 July 1655 by Cornelis de Graeff, the Burgemeester (Burgomaster or Mayor) of Amsterdam.

facts.fact: Jacob van Campen was the main architect from 1648, and the building stands on 13,659 wooden piles.
facts.quote: The main architect was Jacob van Campen, who took control of the construction project in 1648. It was built on 13,659 wooden piles.

facts.fact: Its yellowish sandstone has darkened over time, and a 6 m statue of Atlas carrying the globe crowns the rear.
facts.quote: The sandstone of yellowish hue has darkened considerably in the course of time. Astride the rear of the building is a 6-metre-tall statue of Atlas carrying the Globe on his shoulders.

facts.fact: Designed as a city hall, it lacks the grand entrance usual in royal palaces.
facts.quote: As the building was designed as a city hall, it lacks a grand entrance, which is a rather common feature of most royal palaces.

facts.fact: It is probably Van Campen's best-known work.
facts.quote: His best-known work is probably the large Town Hall of Amsterdam (begun 1648), now the Royal Palace in Dam Square.

facts.fact: It was renovated from 2005 to 2009.
facts.quote: The palace was renovated from 2005 until June 2009, during which, among other things, asbestos was removed.

facts.fact: The Europa building in Brussels is the seat of the European Council and the Council of the EU.
facts.quote: The Europa building is the seat of the European Council and Council of the European Union, located on the Rue de la Loi/Wetstraat in the European Quarter of Brussels, Belgium.

facts.fact: Its defining feature is a multi-storey lantern holding the main meeting rooms, now used as both institutions' emblem.
facts.quote: Its defining feature is the multi-storey lantern-shaped construct holding the main meeting rooms, a representation of which has been adopted by both the European Council and Council of the EU as their official emblems.

facts.fact: It keeps the listed 1920s Art Deco facade of the Résidence Palace and adds Philippe Samyn's contemporary design.
facts.quote: Its exterior combines the Art Deco façade of the original 1920s building, which has been listed since 2004, with the contemporary design of the architect Philippe Samyn.

facts.fact: Samyn and Partners won the 2005 competition with Studio Valle Progettazioni and Buro Happold.
facts.quote: In 2005, it was announced that a team involving the architect Philippe Samyn and Partners (architects and engineers), lead and design partner, in collaboration with Studio Valle Progettazioni (architects), and Buro Happold (engineers) had succeeded in submitting the winning design.

facts.fact: The design built a large glass-cubed atrium joining the two renovated wings of the 1920s L-shaped building.
facts.quote: The design for what was to be later named the Europa building, involved the demolition of the 1960s extension, and the construction of a large glass-cubed atrium connecting the two renovated wings of the original 1920s L-shaped building.

facts.fact: It brings together Samyn's recurring themes: recycled materials (all the wooden frames), photovoltaic panels, a double skin and work with the colourist painter Georges Meurant.
facts.quote: Several recurring elements from the architect's work were present: the use of recycled materials (all wooden frames), photovoltaic panels, double skin, geometric exploration, collaboration with an artist (Georges Meurant, colourist painter), play with opacity and transparency, porous architecture allowing visual appropriation by all.

facts.fact: After setbacks and design changes during the Lisbon Treaty reforms, it was completed in December 2016.
facts.quote: However, due to setbacks and modifications to the design following the evolution of the European Council's needs as an institution during the Lisbon Treaty reforms, the building was completed in December 2016.

facts.fact: Painter Georges Meurant's colour grids cover ceilings, doors, carpets, corridors and lifts.
facts.quote: Meurant's orthogonal polychrome grid designs appear over ceilings in meeting rooms, doors, carpet flooring in conference rooms, as well as in the corridors, press room, catering facilities and elevators.

facts.fact: The Flagey Building, or Radio House, in Ixelles, Brussels, houses the Flagey cultural centre.
facts.quote: The Flagey Building  (French: Bâtiment Flagey; Dutch: Flageygebouw), also known as the Radio House (French: Maison de la Radio; Dutch: Radiohuis), is a building located in Ixelles, a municipality of Brussels, Belgium, housing the Flagey cultural centre.

facts.fact: Joseph Diongre designed it, and it was completed in 1938 in Streamline Moderne, an international style of Art Deco.
facts.quote: The building, parts of which are listed, was designed by the architect Joseph Diongre and completed in 1938 in Streamline Moderne, an international style of Art Deco.

facts.fact: Diongre won a 1933 competition judged by a jury that included Henry van de Velde and Victor Horta.
facts.quote: Henry van de Velde and Victor Horta were on the jury that awarded the prize to Diongre.

facts.fact: It was built as the headquarters of Belgium's first national broadcaster, the INR/NIR.
facts.quote: The competition was launched to create a building to house the first national broadcaster in Belgium, the National Institute of Radio Broadcasting (French: Institut National de Radiodiffusion or INR, Dutch: Nationaal Instituut voor de Radio-omroep or NIR) (1930–1960).

facts.fact: Its ship-like shape earned it the nickname "Packet Boat" (paquebot).
facts.quote: Owing to its shape somewhat resembling a ship, the building is nicknamed "Packet Boat" or "paquebot".

facts.fact: The original design had twelve recording studios in two acoustic towers at the core of the building.
facts.quote: The original design incorporated twelve recording studios, which were built in two acoustic towers forming the core of the building.

facts.fact: It was renovated by architects including Storme Van Ranst and reopened in 2002.
facts.quote: The building was extensively renovated by architects including Storme Van Ranst, and was reopened in 2002.

facts.fact: Its Studio 4, home to the Brussels Philharmonic, is one of the concert halls with the best acoustics worldwide.
facts.quote: Its Studio 4 is one of the concert halls with the best acoustics worldwide, home to the Brussels Philharmonic.

facts.fact: The Royal Greenhouses stand in the Royal Domain of Laeken, joined to the palace through the orangery.
facts.quote: The Royal Greenhouses of Laeken are located within the Royal Domain and are attached to the palace via the orangery.

facts.fact: Commissioned by King Leopold II and first designed by Alphonse Balat, they were built between 1874 and 1905.
facts.quote: They were commissioned by King Leopold II, originally designed by Alphonse Balat, and built between 1874 and 1905.

facts.fact: After Balat died in 1895, Leopold called on Henri Maquet and Charles Girault.
facts.quote: Following Balat's death in 1895, Leopold called upon the architects Henri Maquet and Charles Girault.

facts.fact: The complex is a group of iron-and-glass domed buildings linked by glass-roofed galleries.
facts.quote: It consists of a huge complex of several dome-shaped buildings in iron and glass that are connected by glass-roofed galleries.

facts.fact: Its centrepiece, the domed Winter Garden, is a circular take on the Palm House at Kew.
facts.quote: The centrepiece is the domed Winter Garden, which is a circular interpretation of the Palm House of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.

facts.fact: Working in iron and glass pushed Balat to abandon his classical stance.
facts.quote: Working with new materials like iron and glass, Balat was obliged to abandon his classical stance. This stimulated the architect's imagination.

facts.fact: He gave the steel structures decorative motifs from plants and flowers, a first step toward the Art Nouveau later developed by his apprentice Victor Horta.
facts.quote: In the steel constructions, he introduced decorative motifs derived from plants and flowers. This formed a first step towards Art Nouveau architecture that was further developed by Victor Horta who served as an apprentice of Balat.

facts.fact: The Congo Greenhouse and the domed Iron Church, first meant as the royal chapel, are linked by flowered corridors hundreds of metres long.
facts.quote: The main greenhouses, such as the Congo Greenhouse and the so-called Iron Church, a domed greenhouse, which would originally serve as the royal chapel, are all linked by flowered corridors spanning hundreds of metres.

facts.fact: M Leuven is an art museum in the centre of Leuven, officially opened in 2009.
facts.quote: M Leuven or simply M is an art museum in the inner city of Leuven, Belgium, which was officially opened in 2009.

facts.fact: Before opening, the building was renovated to a design by Belgian architect Stéphane Beel.
facts.quote: Before it was opened in 2009, the M Museum building was renovated after a design by Belgian architect Stéphane Beel.

facts.fact: The design joins historic features and sleek contemporary architecture around a courtyard.
facts.quote: The design integrates historical features and sleek contemporary architecture around a pretty courtyard.

facts.fact: The museum covers 13,500 m².
facts.quote: The total area of the museum is 13,500 square meters.

facts.fact: Its main exhibition space is the former house of mayor Leopold Vander Kelen in the historic centre.
facts.quote: About one century later, the collection was moved to the former private residence of the mayor Leopold Vander Kelen in the historic center of Leuven.  This location is now the principal exhibition space of M Leuven.

facts.fact: Its collection of some 46,000 works runs from late-Gothic painting to 19th-century Flemish masters.
facts.quote: The museum has a collection of some 46,000 works, which range from late-Gothic paintings and sculptures to 16th century local artists such as Jan Rombouts the Elder and Josse van der Baren to 19th-century paintings and sculptures by various Flemish masters including Constantin Meunier, Jef Lambeaux and George Minne.

facts.fact: Leuven Town Hall stands on the Grote Markt opposite St. Peter's Church.
facts.quote: The Town Hall (Dutch: ) of Leuven, Flemish Brabant, Belgium, is a landmark building on that city's Grote Markt (main square), across from the monumental St. Peter's Church.
