facts.quote: The Manila Cathedral was built in the Latin cross (cruciform) layout. Its northwest façade, which is built in the Neo-Romanesque architecture style, is a replica of the façade of the previous cathedral, along with statues of famous saints sculpted in Roman travertine stone.

facts.fact: In 1964 Filipino artist Galo Ocampo made most of its 134 modern stained-glass windows.
facts.quote: In 1964, Filipino artist Galo Ocampo designed and made most of the cathedral's 134 modern stained glass windows.

facts.fact: It closed temporarily in 2012 for repairs, earthquake retrofitting and work to prevent subsidence.
facts.quote: Following the 2012 Negros earthquake and structural concerns, the cathedral temporarily closed on February 7 for repairs, earthquake retrofitting and subsidence prevention.

facts.fact: Its pipe organ remains the largest in Southeast Asia.
facts.quote: Currently, it consists of 6,446 pipes; it remains the largest pipe organ in Southeast Asia.

facts.fact: The Singapore Indoor Stadium is an indoor arena in Kallang, within walking distance of the National Stadium.
facts.quote: The Singapore Indoor Stadium, known exonymously as the Indoor Stadium, is an indoor arena located in Kallang, Singapore. It is within walking distance of the Singapore National Stadium, and collectively form a part of The Kallang.

facts.fact: It holds up to 15,000 people, or 12,000 all seated.
facts.quote: It has a maximum total capacity of 15,000 depending on configuration, with an all-seating configuration of 12,000.

facts.fact: Construction began on 1 January 1985 and cost S$90 million.
facts.quote: Construction began on 1 January 1985, and it was built at a cost of S$90 million.

facts.fact: Japanese architect Kenzo Tange designed it with Raglan Squire & Partners; it has a cone-shaped roof and an arena without pillars.
facts.quote: The arena was designed by Japanese architect Kenzo Tange in partnership with Raglan Squire & Partners, and it has a cone shaped roof and a pillarless arena.

facts.fact: It was completed on 1 March 1987 and opened to the public on 1 July 1988.
facts.quote: It was completed on 1 March 1987 and officially opened to public on 1 July 1988.

facts.fact: Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew officially inaugurated it on 31 December 1989.
facts.quote: On 31 December 1989, Singapore Indoor Stadium was officially opened in an inaugural ceremony by the Prime Minister of Singapore, Lee Kuan Yew.

facts.fact: In 2024 the government revealed plans for a new indoor arena to replace it.
facts.quote: On 7 March 2024, Minister for Culture, Community and Youth Edwin Tong revealed plans for a new indoor arena to replace the existing Indoor Stadium during an outline of the ministry's spending plans.

facts.fact: Ipoh railway station is the main railway terminal of Perak, in the heart of Ipoh.
facts.quote: The Ipoh railway station is a Malaysian train station located in the heart of and named after Ipoh, the capital city of the state of Perak. It serves as the main railway terminal for the state.

facts.fact: Designed by Arthur Benison Hubback, it opened in 1917; locals call it the Taj Mahal of Ipoh, and it houses the Majestic Hotel.
facts.quote: Designed by Arthur Benison Hubback, the current station was officially opened in 1917. Affectionately known as the Taj Mahal of Ipoh by its locals, the building also houses a station hotel called the Majestic Hotel.

facts.fact: Work began in 1914 but, slowed by wartime shortages and rising labour costs, finished only in 1917.
facts.quote: In 1914, construction of a second station and hotel to replace the first station began; dogged by material shortages and escalating costs of labor during World War I, the station was only completed in 1917.

facts.fact: Hubback was a British architect who designed public buildings across British Malaya in colonial Western and Indo-Saracenic styles.
facts.quote: The 1917 station's design was conceptualised by Arthur Benison Hubback, a British architectural assistant to the Director of Public Works credited for designing various public buildings in British Malaya in various vernacular colonial Western styles as well as "Neo-Moorish/Mughal/Indo-Saracenic/Neo-Saracenic" styles that draw influences from British Indian colonial architecture.

facts.fact: Unlike Kuala Lumpur station, it is mainly Edwardian Baroque, with a large central dome over the porte-cochère and deep open-air loggias on both floors; the ground-floor loggia runs the full 183 m frontage.
facts.quote: In contrast to the Kuala Lumpur railway station, the Ipoh station's exterior is more distinctively Western in design, drawing elements of late-Edwardian Baroque architecture and incorporating moderate rustication on the base of the ground floor, opened pointed and arched pediments, extensive use of engaged columns, and a large central dome over the porte-cochère, while integrating vernacular elements such as deep, open air loggias into the ground floor and upper floor of the building (the ground floor's loggia measures at 183 metres, the length of the station's frontage).

facts.fact: Small Indo-Saracenic chhatris top the corner columns on both sides.
facts.quote: In spite of its overall aesthetics, elements of Indo-Saracenic architecture are still found in the form of miniature chhatris towering over corner support columns on both sides of the structure.

facts.fact: The station's layout stayed largely unchanged for over 80 years.
facts.quote: For over 80 years, throughout the operational years of the FMSR and its eventual successor, Keretapi Tanah Melayu (Malayan Railways), the station's overall layout has remained largely unchanged since its construction due to minimal upgrading exercises throughout the wider Peninsular Malaysian railway network.

facts.fact: Jakarta Kota is a major terminus station in Kota Tua, Jakarta's old city core.
facts.quote: Jakarta Kota Station (Indonesian: Stasiun Jakarta Kota, station code: JAKK) is a railway station, located in the old city core of Kota Tua, Jakarta, Indonesia.

facts.fact: The old station was closed in 1923 and rebuilt between 1926 and 1929.
facts.quote: The southern BOS station was closed in 1923, and was rebuilt between 1926 and 1929, during which all rail services were temporarily taken over by the Batavia North station.

facts.fact: The building was designed in 1927–1928 by Asselbergs, Frans Ghijsels and Hes of the AIA firm in Batavia.
facts.quote: The station building was designed in 1927–1928 by the architects Asselbergs, Frans Johan Louwrens Ghijsels, and Hes from the architectural company Algemeen Ingenieurs-en Architectenbureau (AIA) in Batavia.

facts.fact: It opened on 8 October 1929.
facts.quote: The new and current building was officially opened on 8 October 1929 with a private ceremony by the company staff.

facts.fact: It is Ghijsels' masterpiece of the Het Indische Bouwen idea, blending Western Art Deco with local traditional forms.
facts.quote: The architecture is Ghijsels' masterpiece known as the Het Indische Bouwen expression, which is a combination of western modern art deco structures and techniques combined with local traditional forms.

facts.fact: A barrel-vault roof covers the main entrance and hall.
facts.quote: The main entrance and hall are characterized by a barrel vault roof with openings horizontally composed with the top dominated by vertical units (lunettes).

facts.fact: The hall walls are rough brown ceramic inside, and the floors are teak and grey wood.
facts.quote: The inside wall of the hall is finished with rough-textured brown ceramic and the outside wall at the bottom of the whole building was covered with green-yellowish plaster. The station floor uses yellow teak and grey wood, and for the platform floor yellow waffle teakwood is used.

facts.fact: It was designated cultural heritage in 1993.
facts.quote: Jakarta Kota Station was finally designated as a cultural heritage through Special Capital Region of Jakarta Governor Decree No. 475 in 1993.

facts.fact: Swan and Maclaren built the Sultan Mosque between 1924 and 1928.
facts.quote: In the years between World Wars I and II, the firm continued to lead the local market with projects such as the Sultan Mosque (1924–28), Ocean Building (1923), Hongkong Bank Chambers (now HSBC Building) (1925), Prinsep Street Presbyterian Church (1930) and the Singapore Turf Club (1934).

facts.fact: Irish architect Denis Santry, a partner at Swan & Maclaren from 1918, was the architect of the Sultan Mosque.
facts.quote: Santry came to Singapore in 1918 and joined architectural firm Swan & Maclaren as a partner. While in Singapore, he served as the architect of several prominent buildings and monuments, including the Sultan Mosque, The Cenotaph, the Maritime Building, the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank Building and the Telok Ayer Chinese Methodist Church.

facts.fact: Wat Rong Khun, the White Temple, is a privately owned contemporary art exhibit in the style of a Buddhist temple, outside Chiang Rai.
facts.quote: Wat Rong Khun (Thai: วัดร่องขุ่น), better known as the White Temple, is a contemporary, privately owned art exhibit in the style of a Buddhist temple in Pa O Don Chai, Mueang District, Chiang Rai province, Thailand.

facts.fact: It was designed and built by national artist Chalermchai Kositpipat, who opened it to visitors in 1997.
facts.quote: The White Temple was created by master Chalermchai Kositpipat, the national artist who designed, constructed, and opened it to visitors in 1997.

facts.fact: The main structure is a concrete frame with a wooden roof.
facts.quote: The primary structure of the temple is made of a basic concrete frame and a wooden roof.

facts.fact: Its sparkle, which looks like porcelain from afar, comes from whitewash mixed with transparent mirrored chips.
facts.quote: Viewed from a distance, it appears to be crafted from sparkling porcelain, but on closer inspection it becomes evident that the dazzling effect is achieved through a blend of whitewash and transparent mirrored chips.

facts.fact: The artist rebuilt the run-down original temple with his own money.
facts.quote: Chalermchai Kositpipat, a local artist from Chiang Rai, decided to completely rebuild the temple and fund the project with his own money.

facts.fact: Work is ongoing and not expected to finish until 2070.
facts.quote: Today the works are ongoing, but are not expected to be completed until 2070.

facts.fact: The ubosot is reached by a bridge over a lake, in front of which hundreds of reaching hands symbolise unrestrained desire.
facts.quote: The main building at the white temple, the ubosot, is reached by crossing a bridge over a small lake. In front of the bridge are hundreds of outreaching hands that symbolize unrestrained desire.

facts.fact: The all-white ubosot has mirrored glass set into its exterior and uses classic Thai elements such as a three-tiered roof and Nāga serpents.
facts.quote: The principal building, the ubosot, is an all-white building with fragments of mirrored glass embedded in its exterior. It embodies design elements from classic Thai architecture, such as the three-tiered roof and abundant use of Nāga serpents.

facts.fact: The Inland Steel Building is a 101 m skyscraper at 30 West Monroe Street in Chicago.
facts.quote: The Inland Steel Building is a 332-foot-tall (101 m) skyscraper at 30 West Monroe Street in Chicago, Illinois, United States.

facts.fact: Built from 1956 to 1958, it was designed by Bruce Graham and Walter Netsch of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill in the International Style.
facts.quote: Constructed from 1956 to 1958, the building was designed by Bruce Graham and Walter Netsch of the architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) in the International Style.

facts.fact: It was the Inland Steel Company's headquarters and one of the first skyscrapers built in the Chicago Loop after World War II.
facts.quote: It was originally the headquarters of the Inland Steel Company and was one of the first skyscrapers to be built in the Chicago Loop since World War II.

facts.fact: It is a Chicago Landmark and is on the National Register of Historic Places.
facts.quote: The Inland Steel Building is designated a Chicago Landmark and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.fact: It has two masses: a 19-storey main block and a 25-storey mechanical tower to the east.
facts.quote: The Inland Steel Building consists of two distinct masses: a 19-story main structure at the corner of Monroe and Dearborn, and a 25-story mechanical tower to the east.

facts.fact: The curtain wall pairs green-tinted glass with stainless steel spandrels, columns and mullions.
facts.quote: The main building's facade consists of a curtain wall with green-tinted glass and stainless steel spandrel panels, columns, and mullions.

facts.fact: The façade columns carry the whole weight, so most of the interior has no columns.
facts.quote: The facade's columns carry the building's entire weight, allowing the majority of the spaces inside to be designed without any interior columns.

facts.fact: All stairs, lifts and utility ducts are in the separate mechanical tower.
facts.quote: The mechanical tower contains all the stairs, elevators, and utility ducts.

facts.fact: The architects rejected black steel columns as too close to Mies van der Rohe's towers.
facts.quote: The architects also contemplated using black steel for the exterior columns, but decided against it, on the basis that it was too similar to Ludwig Mies van der Rohe's skyscrapers.

facts.fact: The Kluczynski Federal Building is a 45-storey skyscraper by Mies van der Rohe, completed in 1974 as the last part of Chicago's Federal Center.
facts.quote: The 45-story structure was designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and completed in 1974 as the last portion of the new Federal Center.

facts.fact: It is one of three Mies buildings around Federal Center Plaza, with the Loop Station Post Office and the Dirksen Courthouse.
facts.quote: This is one of three buildings by Mies in the Federal Center Plaza complex: the others are the Loop Station Post Office and the Everett McKinley Dirksen United States Courthouse.

facts.fact: It has a steel frame and about 110,000 m2 of space.
facts.quote: The John C. Kluczynski Building is constructed of a steel frame and contains 1,200,000 sq ft (110,000 m2) of space.

facts.fact: The exterior is bronze-tinted glass in aluminium frames, with black-painted steel spandrels and projecting I-beam mullions.
facts.quote: The exterior is sheathed in bronze-tinted glass set into bright aluminum frames. Beneath the windows are steel spandrel panels painted flat black and windows are separated horizontally by steel mullions of projecting steel I-beams also painted black.

facts.fact: The two-storey lobby is set back so that a colonnade circles the building at street level.
facts.quote: The two-story lobby is recessed allowing for a colonnade or pilotis to encircle the building at street level.

facts.fact: The whole complex follows a 28 ft (8.5 m) grid, with paving seams running from the plaza into the lobbies.
facts.quote: The entire complex is based on a 28 ft (8.5 m) grid pattern so that seams of the granite pavers in the plaza extend into the building lobbies and up the sides to create unity among the three structures.

facts.fact: Alexander Calder's 16 m red steel sculpture Flamingo was unveiled on the plaza on 24 October 1974.
facts.quote: Alexander Calder's sculpture Flamingo, a 53-foot  (16 m) red steel sculpture, was unveiled on the plaza October 24, 1974.

facts.fact: The Reliance Building is a skyscraper at 1 West Washington Street in Chicago's Loop.
facts.quote: The Reliance Building is a skyscraper at 1 West Washington Street in the Loop community area of Chicago, Illinois.

facts.fact: John Root of Burnham and Root designed the first floor and basement in 1890; Charles B. Atwood completed the rest in 1895.
facts.quote: The first floor and basement were designed by John Root of the Burnham and Root architectural firm in 1890, while the rest of the building was completed by Charles B. Atwood in 1895.

facts.fact: It was the first skyscraper with large plate-glass windows over most of its surface, a feature that became dominant in the 20th century.
facts.quote: It is the first skyscraper to have large plate glass windows covering the majority of its surface area—a design feature that became dominant in the 20th century.

facts.fact: Atwood clad it in white glazed architectural terra cotta.
facts.quote: After raising the original building's remaining three floors Atwood used white glazed architectural terra-cotta cladding, a feature that would later become strongly associated with him following his works for the World's Columbian Exposition in 1893.

facts.fact: The steel frame of the top ten floors went up in fifteen days in 1895.
facts.quote: The steel framing on the top ten floors was completed over fifteen days, from July 16 to August 1, 1895.

facts.fact: Its stacked projecting bay windows and terra-cotta cladding give an effect of great lightness, and it has been called proto-Modernist.
facts.quote: The Reliance Building has been called "proto-Modernist" in its lack of the hierarchy found in Classical facades.  Its stacks of projecting bay windows and terra-cotta cladding create an effect of extraordinary lightness.

facts.fact: It directly foreshadowed Mies van der Rohe's 1921 all-glass Friedrichstrasse skyscraper proposal.
facts.quote: It was a direct precursor of the all-glass Friedrichstrasse skyscraper proposed by Mies van der Rohe in 1921.

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1970 and became a National Historic Landmark in 1976.
facts.quote: The Reliance Building was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1970 and designated a National Historic Landmark in 1976.

facts.fact: Its modernist tower mainly houses Cook County courtrooms and offices, plus office space for the city and county.
facts.quote: The Center's modernist skyscraper primarily houses offices and courtrooms for the Cook County Circuit Courts, Cook County State's Attorney and additional office space for the City and the County.

facts.fact: Its open granite plaza is used for gatherings, protests and events and holds the Chicago Picasso.
facts.quote: The open granite-paved plaza used for gatherings, protests, and events is also the site of the Chicago Picasso, a gift to the city from the artist.

facts.fact: It was designed in the International Style of the Second Chicago School by Jacques Brownson of C. F. Murphy Associates, with SOM and Loebl, Schlossman, Bennett & Dart, and completed in 1965.
facts.quote: The main building was designed in the International Style of the Second Chicago School by Jacques Brownson of the firm C. F. Murphy Associates as supervising architects, with Skidmore, Owings & Merrill and Loebl, Schlossman, Bennett & Dart as associated architects, and was completed in 1965.

facts.fact: When finished it was Chicago's tallest building, until the John Hancock Center four years later.
facts.quote: At the time it was the tallest building in Chicago, but only held this title for four years until the John Hancock Center was completed.

facts.fact: The 198 m, 31-storey building is clad in Cor-Ten weathering steel, which rusts to a red-brown colour.
facts.quote: The 648-foot (198 m), thirty-one story building features Cor-Ten, a self-weathering steel.  Cor-Ten was designed to rust, actually strengthening the structure and giving the building its distinctive red and brown color.

facts.fact: With 30 floors above a double-height lobby, it is the world's tallest flat-roofed building with fewer than 40 storeys.
facts.quote: The Daley Center has 30 floors above its double height lobby, and is the tallest flat-roofed building in the world with fewer than 40 stories (a typical 648-foot (198 m) building, the height of Daley Center, would have 50–60 stories).

facts.fact: It holds more than 120 court and hearing rooms.
facts.quote: The Richard J. Daley Center houses more than 120 court and hearing rooms as well as the Cook County Law Library, offices of the Clerk of the Circuit Court, and certain court-related divisions of the Sheriff's Department.

facts.fact: The Rookery is a historic office building at 209 South LaSalle Street in Chicago's Loop.
facts.quote: The Rookery Building is a historic office building at 209 South LaSalle Street in the Loop community area of downtown Chicago, Illinois, United States.

facts.fact: Burnham and Root completed it in 1888; it is considered one of their masterpieces and once held their offices.
facts.quote: Completed by architects Daniel Burnham and John Wellborn Root of Burnham and Root in 1888, it is considered one of their masterpiece buildings, and was once the location of their offices.

facts.fact: At 12 storeys and 55 m, it is considered the oldest standing high-rise in Chicago, with load-bearing outer walls and an inner steel frame.
facts.quote: The building is 181 feet (55 m) in height, twelve stories tall, and is considered the oldest standing high-rise in Chicago. It features exterior load-bearing walls and an interior steel frame.

facts.fact: Burnham and Root mixed modern techniques such as metal framing, fireproofing, lifts and plate glass with brick façades and rich ornament.
facts.quote: In their design for the building, Burnham and Root mixed modern building techniques, such as metal framing, fireproofing, elevators and plate glass, with traditional ones, such as brick facades and elaborate ornamentation.

facts.fact: Root designed a grillage foundation of iron rails and beams set crosswise in concrete to carry the weight on soft soil.
facts.quote: Root designed a grillage foundation, in which iron rails and the structural beams are combined in a crisscross pattern and encased in concrete to support the building's immense weight without heavy foundation stones.

facts.fact: Its mix of iron framing and masonry bearing walls marked a step in the move from masonry to steel-skeleton structures.
facts.quote: The building uses a combination of cast and wrought iron framing and masonry bearing walls. This marked a transitional moment in a switch from masonry to steel skeleton structures, and, according to the architectural critic Paul Goldberger, was a precursor to the steel frames of early skyscrapers.

facts.fact: A two-storey central light court, clad in white terracotta under a skylight of 5,000 glass panes, lights the interior offices.
facts.quote: The light court, clad in white terracotta, provides natural illumination for the interior offices. The skylight atop the light court is composed of 5,000 glass panes.

facts.fact: Frank Lloyd Wright redesigned the lobby in 1905 in his Prairie style; it is his only work in the Loop.
facts.quote: The lobby, redesigned by Frank Lloyd Wright in 1905, recast the entryway in his Prairie style, with a simple, modern-style lighting design. Wright's Rookery atrium is his only work on any building in the Chicago Loop, as most of his work in the Chicago metropolitan area was in outlying neighborhoods or the suburbs.

facts.fact: It is a Chicago Landmark and a National Historic Landmark.
facts.quote: The building is designated a Chicago Landmark, and it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places as a National Historic Landmark.

facts.fact: The Canadian Centre for Architecture's Eero Saarinen collection documents the North Christian Church in Columbus, Indiana.
facts.quote: The Eero Saarinen collection at the Canadian Centre for Architecture documents eight built projects, including the old Athens airport in Greece, the former US Embassy Chanceries in Oslo, Norway and London, England, corporate projects for John Deere, CBS, and IBM, and the North Christian Church in Columbus, Indiana.

facts.fact: The North Christian Church is among the seven buildings in Columbus designated National Historic Landmarks.
facts.quote: The First Christian Church is one of seven buildings in Columbus designated as National Historic Landmarks. The others are The Republic Newspaper Office, the Mabel McDowell Adult Education Center, the Miller House, the Irwin Union Bank Building, the North Christian Church, and the First Baptist Church.

facts.fact: Its congregation split off from the First Christian Church.
facts.quote: Over the years, several congregations have split from the First Christian Church, including the short-lived Central Christian Church and the North Christian Church.

facts.fact: In 1958 Paul Rudolph began designing a new building to extend Sarasota High School's Collegiate Gothic building.
facts.quote: In 1958, American architect Paul Rudolph began to design a new Sarasota High School building to expand on the Collegiate Gothic building.

facts.fact: The campus combines a 1926 Collegiate Gothic building by M. Leo Elliott with Rudolph's mid-century building of 1958–1959.
facts.quote: The current campus, consisting of two buildings — a 60,000-square-foot (5,600 m2) 1926 Collegiate Gothic structure designed by M. Leo Elliott and a 20,000-square-foot (1,900 m2) mid-century building by Paul Rudolph added in 1958-1959.

facts.fact: Rudolph composed the addition of folding concrete planes.
facts.quote: To contrast the steel complex design that was just completed at Riverview High, Rudolph designed the new addition as a composition of folding concrete planes.

facts.fact: Horizontal plates and vertical piers suit Sarasota's climate, with classrooms along an open-air axis for natural ventilation.
facts.quote: He developed a system of horizontal plates and vertical piers to work well with the local Sarasota climate, which included providing natural ventilation to classrooms by placing them along an open-air axis.

facts.fact: The design won an AIA Award of Merit in 1962.
facts.quote: This design resulted in Rudolph receiving the prestigious Award of Merit from the American Institute of Architects Honor Awards Program in 1962.

facts.fact: It is a concrete building with large overhanging sunshades and naturally ventilated outdoor corridors.
facts.quote: Another school building design in Sarasota was Rudolph's 1960 addition to Sarasota High School, a concrete structure that utilized large overhanging sunshades and "internal" yet outside corridors with natural ventilation.

facts.fact: Rudolph's addition was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 26 June 2012.
facts.quote:
On June 26, 2012, Paul Rudolph’s SHS Addition was listed 
on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.fact: After 50 years as classrooms, Rudolph's building became the campus 'front door' and home of its administrative offices.
facts.quote: After 50 years as classrooms, it was repurposed to become the “front door” of the entire campus and the home of the administrative offices.

facts.fact: Frank Lloyd Wright designed the Graycliff estate in 1926, and it was built between 1926 and 1931.
facts.quote: The Graycliff estate was designed by Frank Lloyd Wright in 1926, and built between 1926 and 1931.

facts.fact: It sits on a bluff above Lake Erie and is one of the most ambitious summer estates Wright designed.
facts.quote: Situated on a bluff overlooking Lake Erie with sweeping views of downtown Buffalo and the Ontario shore, It is one of the most ambitious and extensive summer estates Wright designed.

facts.fact: It was the second of two complexes Wright designed for the Martins, after their city home, the Martin House Complex.
facts.quote: Graycliff was the second of two complexes Frank Lloyd Wright designed for the couple, the first being the Martin House Complex, their city residence.

facts.fact: It is the only Wright building in stone between Taliesin (1925) and Fallingwater (1936).
facts.quote: Graycliff is one of only five of Frank Lloyd Wright's designs that were built between 1925 and 1935, and the only Wright-designed structure built between Taliesin (1925) and Fallingwater (1936) using stone.

facts.fact: It is a complex of three buildings set in an 8.5-acre landscape.
facts.quote: Graycliff is a complex of three buildings integrated within an 8.5-acre (34,000 m2) landscape.

facts.fact: The main house has two stone sections framing a glass-walled centre, so you can see through the building to the lake.
facts.quote: The largest building, the main "Isabelle R. Martin House," is perhaps most remarkable for its two stone veneered sections framing a central pavilion-like center of transparent glass walls, allowing visitors to actually see through the building itself to the lake beyond, revolutionary for a 1926 design.

facts.fact: The buildings use stone from the lake's edge, ochre stucco and red cedar shingle roofs.
facts.quote: Like the other two buildings, it is constructed of stone found at the lake's edge, ocher stucco, and a red cedar shingle roof.

facts.fact: Graycliff is a New York State Landmark and is on the National Register of Historic Places.
facts.quote: Graycliff is a New York State Landmark and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.fact: Frank Lloyd Wright designed the house in Madison for journalist Herbert Jacobs's family; finished in 1937, it is sometimes cited as his first Usonian house.
facts.quote: Designed by the architect Frank Lloyd Wright for the family of the journalist Herbert Jacobs, it was completed in 1937 and is sometimes cited as Wright's first Usonian-style house.

facts.fact: It is a single-storey, L-shaped house of 1,550 sq ft on a slope towards Lake Wingra.
facts.quote: The house is a single-story, L-shaped structure covering 1,550 square feet (144 m2). It sits on a slope that descends toward Lake Wingra to the southeast.

facts.fact: Jacobs asked Wright in August 1936 for a house costing no more than $5,000.
facts.quote: In August 1936, Jacobs asked Wright to design a house costing no more than $5,000; the architect devised the initial plans within two months.

facts.fact: The plan turns away from the street and partly wraps a rear garden at the centre of the site.
facts.quote: The floor plan faces away from the street, partially surrounding a rear garden, which is geographically at the center of the site.

facts.fact: The street side is a wall of brick, boards and battens, while large windows and glass doors face the garden.
facts.quote: The facade includes a wall of bricks, boards, and battens facing the street, alongside large windows and glass doors facing a rear garden.

facts.fact: It sits on a concrete pad with radiant heating in the floor, under three levels of flat roofs with deep eaves.
facts.quote: The house has a concrete pad foundation, with a radiant heating system embedded into the floor, and is covered by three levels of flat roofs with protruding eaves.

facts.fact: Its board-and-batten walls, radiant heating and modular floor grid were later widely used.
facts.quote: Several of its architectural features were later widely used, including its board-and-batten walls, radiant heating system, and modular floor grid.

facts.fact: It became a National Historic Landmark in 2003 and part of the World Heritage Site of Wright's 20th-century architecture in 2019.
facts.quote: The Jacobs First House was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974 and designated as a National Historic Landmark in 2003. It was designated as part of The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright, a World Heritage Site, in 2019.

facts.fact: The house belongs to the National Trust for Historic Preservation and has been moved twice; it now stands at Woodlawn Plantation, Alexandria, Virginia.
facts.quote: The house, which belongs to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, has been relocated twice and sits on the grounds of Woodlawn Plantation, Alexandria, Virginia.

facts.fact: Commissioned in 1939 by journalist Loren Pope, it was one of Wright's first Usonian houses and was completed in 1941 in Falls Church.
facts.quote: Commissioned in 1939 by journalist Loren Pope and his wife Charlotte Pope, the Pope–Leighey House was one of the first Usonian houses designed by Frank Lloyd Wright. It was completed in 1941, located at 1005 Locust Street, Falls Church, Virginia.

facts.fact: To fit the Popes' budget, Wright cut the plan from 1,800 to 1,200 sq ft.
facts.quote: Mindful of the Popes' financial limitations, Wright scaled down the plan from 1,800 square feet to 1,200 square feet.

facts.fact: It shows key Usonian features: an L shape, a flat roof, natural materials, cantilevers and indoor-outdoor links.
facts.quote: The house features many of the key elements of Usonian architecture, including an L shape, a flat roof, natural building materials, cantilevered structure (particularly in the carport), and an integration of the outdoors with the indoors.

facts.fact: The house is one storey on two levels to follow the slope, and its roof rests on three brick pillars.
facts.quote: The house is one story, but it has two levels to accommodate the natural slope of the land. The original plans had included a workshop, but it had to be removed when Wright downsized the design for affordability. The roof is held up by three brick pillars.

facts.fact: Clerestory windows, vents and a concrete floor regulate temperature naturally, without air conditioning.
facts.quote: These windows, combined with vents and a concrete floor, enable natural regulation of temperature in the house without air conditioning, which was notably innovative at the time of design.

facts.fact: The brick and wood are left unpainted, treated with clear wax.
facts.quote: The brick and wood used throughout the house are not painted but rather treated with clear wax, which accentuates their natural qualities.

facts.fact: In 1995 the house was moved again, only 30 feet, at a cost of $500,000.
facts.quote: In 1995, the house was again relocated to a spot only 30 feet (9.1 m) away, at a cost of $500,000.

facts.fact: Completed in 1962, it is considered one of the best-known mid-century modern buildings in Des Moines.
facts.quote: Completed in 1962, it is considered to be "one of the most well-known examples of mid-century modern architecture in Des Moines."

facts.fact: It was designed by Mies van der Rohe and is one of the first steel-and-glass modernist buildings downtown.
facts.quote: It was designed by the prominent Chicago architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and it is one of the first steel and glass modernist buildings in the city's downtown.

facts.fact: A first design hung the roof from two lengthwise trusses, as at IIT in Chicago.
facts.quote: Initially, the roof was designed to be suspended from two lengthwise trusses, similar van der Rohe's designs at the Illinois Institute of Technology in Chicago.

facts.fact: The built design is simpler: a steel frame with glass infill on a base of granite and travertine.
facts.quote: That design was abandoned for a simpler and more direct design that features a steel-frame, glass-infill, and granite and travertine marble on the base.

facts.fact: The three-storey building is 12.27 m tall.
facts.quote: The three-story building rises to the height of 40.25 feet (12.27 m).

facts.fact: Donated to the Diocese of Des Moines in 1992, it became its headquarters.
facts.quote: In 1992 philanthropist Ed Ochylski acquired it and donated it to the Diocese of Des Moines, which converted it into its headquarters.

facts.fact: It was renovated in 2016–2017 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2017.
facts.quote: From 2016 to 2017, the building underwent a $10 million renovation. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2017.

facts.fact: The bank in Owatonna, Minnesota, was designed by Louis Sullivan with decorative elements by George Elmslie.
facts.quote: The National Farmers' Bank of Owatonna, Minnesota, United States, is a historic bank building designed by Louis Sullivan, with decorative elements by George Elmslie.

facts.fact: Built in 1908, it was the first of Sullivan's 'jewel box' banks.
facts.quote: It was built in 1908, and was the first of Sullivan's "jewel box" bank designs.

facts.fact: It is clad in red brick with green terra-cotta bands, with two large arches on its street fronts.
facts.quote: The building is clad in red brick with green terra cotta bands, and features two large arches on its street-facing facades.

facts.fact: Inside are stained-glass windows by Louis J. Millet, a mural by Oskar Gross and four huge cast-iron electroliers by Elmslie.
facts.quote: Internal elements include two stained-glass windows designed by Louis J. Millet, a mural by Oskar Gross, and four immense cast iron electroliers designed by Elmslie and cast by Winslow Brothers Company.

facts.fact: The bank's officers wanted a fresh idea for a bank, feeling conventional bank architecture would not meet their needs.
facts.quote: The officers of the National Farmers' Bank sought Sullivan out, in part because they wanted a fresh idea of a bank building that would suit their specific needs, and they felt that conventional bank architecture of the time would not meet those.

facts.fact: A 1940 remodel destroyed much of the interior, later restored in 1958 and 1976–1981.
facts.quote: The bank was remodeled in 1940, and many of the interior architectural elements were destroyed. Subsequent work in 1958 and from 1976 to 1981 restored it to its original grandeur.

facts.fact: It became a National Historic Landmark on 7 January 1976.
facts.quote: On January 7, 1976, it was recognized as a National Historic Landmark for its architectural significance.
